45601: Gifts and Talents: Expression, Not Just a Tool
45602: How Christians can use their gifts, why evangelicals often turned every gift into a tool for evangelism, and what a fuller biblical picture looks like
45603: Every ability you have, from teaching a Bible study to fixing an engine or writing a song, is a gift from God (1 Cor 4:7). The Bible gives gifts several purposes at once: they reflect the image of the Creator, they serve and build up other people, they honour God as worship, and they can point people to Christ. Many evangelicals, out of real love for the lost and a sense of urgency, came to treat gifts mainly as tools for sharing the gospel, so that a song or a business or a painting only 'counted' if it led to a conversation about Jesus. That instinct protects something important: the gospel must be spoken, and people do need to hear it (Rom 10:14-15). But when it becomes the only measure, it can split life into 'sacred' and 'secular', turn art into advertising, and make neighbours into projects. The healthier view held by many evangelical, Catholic, Orthodox and Reformed teachers is that gifts are both expression and witness: done well and in love, they glorify God in themselves, and that same faithful work often opens the door for words.
45604: The first gifts in the Bible are creative and practical: God fills Bezalel with his Spirit to make beautiful things for worship (Exod 31:1-6), long before any list of 'spiritual gifts'.
45605: In the parable, a 'talent' was a large sum of money, not a natural ability; the English meaning of 'talent' grew out of later readings of the parable (Matt 25:14-30).
45606: Paul gives Spirit gifts a clear purpose: love and the building up of the body (1 Cor 12:7, 1 Cor 14:12), and he says gifts without love are worth nothing (1 Cor 13:1-3).
45607: Ordinary work is service to God and neighbour (Col 3:23-24); Luther and the Reformers taught that a farmer or a mother is as truly called as a priest.
45608: The evangelistic framing of gifts has real roots: urgency about eternity, love for people, the Great Commission and revivalist history. It deserves understanding, not mockery.
45609: Its costs are also real: a sacred/secular divide, art used as propaganda, people treated as targets, guilt over 'non-ministry' work, and weak craft.
45610: The strongest evangelical answers (Lausanne, Stott, Keller, Crouch) hold together that proclamation matters uniquely and that good work and beauty matter in themselves.
45611: The Hebrew word avodah means both work and worship, and the Sabbath reminds us that our worth is not our output.
45612: Creation and the image of God
45618: How gifts, creation, love and mission connect
45619: This map shows how the Bible ties gifts to creation, to the Spirit, to work and to mission. Follow the arrows: gifts begin in the image of God, are shaped by love, and flow out as worship, service and witness. The 'sacred/secular divide' node shows where the connections were later broken.
45620: Humans are made in God's image and likeness (Gen 1:26-27). In context this means, at least, that humans represent God in the world and share in his creative, ordering rule. A creative God makes creative creatures, so human making is part of what it means to be human, not a distraction from it.
45622: God tells the first humans to fill the earth and rule it (Gen 1:28) and places Adam in the garden 'to work it and keep it' (Gen 2:15). Theologians call this the 'cultural mandate': the call to develop the world's potential through work, culture and care. Adam naming the animals is an early picture of ordering and understanding creation.
45625: The first person in the Bible said to be 'filled with the Spirit of God' is an artist: Bezalel, gifted with skill in metal, stone, wood and design to build the tabernacle (Exod 31:1-6). God also gives him and Oholiab the ability to teach others (Exod 35:34). Craft is a Spirit gift.
45628: In Hebrew the same word, chokmah, means both 'wisdom' and 'skill'. The craftsmen of the tabernacle are called 'wise-hearted'. Proverbs praises the person skilled in work who will stand before kings (Prov 22:29), and Isaiah says the farmer's know-how is taught by God (Isa 28:26).
45630: David organises skilled musicians for the temple, who 'prophesy' with lyres and cymbals (1 Chr 25:1-7). The Psalms ask for skilful playing (Ps 33:3). Music in Israel is first worship and expression of lament and joy, and it also declares God's deeds among the nations (Ps 96:3).
45636: Paul and Peter list gifts (charismata, 'grace-gifts') in Rom 12:6-8, 1 Cor 12:8-10 and 12:28-30, Eph 4:11 and 1 Pet 4:10-11. The lists differ and overlap, which suggests they are samples, not a complete catalogue. They include both 'supernatural' gifts (healing, tongues) and ordinary ones (giving, leading, mercy).
45637: Gifts differ from person to person, but the fruit of the Spirit (love, joy, peace and the rest) is meant to grow in everyone (Gal 5:22-23). Gifts describe what we do for others; fruit describes who we are becoming. Gifts without fruit can harm the church.
45639: Paul places his great chapter on love between two chapters on gifts. Prophecy, knowledge, faith and even self-sacrifice without love are 'nothing' (1 Cor 13:1-3). Love is the motive and the measure of every gift, and it outlasts them all (1 Cor 13:8-13).
45641: Gifts are given 'for the common good' (1 Cor 12:7). The church is one body with many parts, and the weaker-seeming parts are indispensable (1 Cor 12:21-26). No gift is for private display; each serves the whole.
45644: Vocation means 'calling'. Paul tells believers to remain in the station in which they were called and to serve God there (1 Cor 7:17-24), and to work heartily 'as for the Lord' (Col 3:23-24). The Reformers used this to argue that every honest occupation is a calling from God.
45646: God gives good gifts to all people, believers or not: rain, harvests, skill and wisdom (Matt 5:45, Acts 14:17). Culture first appears in Cain's line (music, metalwork, herding, Gen 4:20-22). Reformed theology calls this 'common grace': talent is God's gift even where he is not acknowledged.
45648: God made trees 'pleasant to the sight' as well as good for food (Gen 2:9) and ordered priestly garments 'for glory and for beauty' (Exod 28:2). Beauty is not only decoration for a message; it reflects God's own goodness (Ps 27:4). Paul tells believers to think about whatever is lovely (Phil 4:8).
45649: Paul calls offering our whole bodies to God our 'reasonable' or 'spiritual worship' (Rom 12:1). Hebrews names praise and also doing good and sharing as sacrifices pleasing to God (Heb 13:15-16). Worship is wider than singing: it includes faithful work and love.
45651: The Hebrew root avad gives avodah, which means work, service and worship. Adam is to 'work' (avad) the garden (Gen 2:15); Israel is to 'serve' (avad) God at Sinai (Exod 3:12); the Levites perform the 'service' of the sanctuary (Num 8:11). The language itself refuses a split between labour and worship.
45652: Immediately after naming Bezalel, God commands the Sabbath (Exod 31:12-17): even holy work stops. Work is good, but it is not our identity or our saviour. Rest declares that God, not our productivity, holds the world together.
45653: Jesus says people will see good works and glorify the Father (Matt 5:16). Peter says honourable conduct among outsiders can lead them to glorify God (1 Pet 2:12). Witness includes how we live and work, and it also includes being ready to give a reason for our hope (1 Pet 3:15).
45654: The risen Jesus sends his disciples to make disciples of all nations, baptising and teaching them (Matt 28:18-20), and to be his witnesses to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8). For many evangelicals this command defines the church's central task.
45656: Evangelism is announcing the good news of Jesus and calling people to trust him. Paul insists that people cannot believe without hearing (Rom 10:14-15) and adapts his life to win others (1 Cor 9:19-23). Some people have a particular gift as evangelists (Eph 4:11), but all believers can speak of their hope.
45659: The idea that some activities (prayer, preaching, missions) are 'spiritual' while others (business, art, housework) are merely 'secular'. It has ancient roots in a two-tier view of Christian life and modern forms in evangelical culture. The Lausanne Cape Town Commitment (2010) named it a major obstacle to mission.
45661: In the parable of the talents, a master entrusts large sums of money to servants according to their ability (Matt 25:14-30). A 'talent' was a weight of silver worth many years of wages. The parable is about faithfulness with what the master entrusts, and later readers applied it to every kind of ability.
45663: Jesus joins love of God and love of neighbour as the two great commandments (Matt 22:37-40). Much of our daily work is how we love neighbours: growing food, healing, teaching, building. The Good Samaritan helps without first asking about belief (Luke 10:25-37).
45664: Revelation pictures the kings of the earth bringing 'the glory and honour of the nations' into the new Jerusalem (Rev 21:24-26), echoing Isa 60. Many interpreters read this as human culture, purified, entering God's renewed world. Others read it more modestly as the nations' worship. Paul says labour 'in the Lord' is not in vain (1 Cor 15:58).
45666: Some Christians say only souls and God's word last forever, so only work that saves souls truly matters. Others point to bodily resurrection and a renewed earth (Rom 8:19-21) and to works that 'follow' believers (Rev 14:13). Your answer to 'what lasts?' shapes how you value gifts.
45668: Charisma comes from charis, grace. A gift is first something received, not achieved: 'What do you have that you did not receive?' (1 Cor 4:7). This frees people from boasting and from despair, and it creates gratitude and a relationship with the Giver.
45700: A path for any gift, whether it is preaching, carpentry, accounting or song-writing. The steps are not a ladder you climb once; most people walk around this circle many times.
45702: Notice what you do well, what others thank you for, and what you love doing. Gifts are often confirmed by the community rather than self-declared (1 Tim 4:14).
45703: What do people repeatedly ask me to help with?
45704: What work makes me lose track of time?
45705: Has my church or my workplace confirmed this ability?
45707: A gift is received, not earned (1 Cor 4:7). That removes both pride and false modesty, and it turns the gift into a relationship of thanks with the Giver.
45708: Do I treat this ability as mine to boast about?
45709: Do I despise it because it seems ordinary?
45710: Can I thank God for it by name?
45712: Bezalel was gifted and also trained and taught others (Exod 35:34). Paul tells Timothy to fan his gift into flame and practise it (2 Tim 1:6, 1 Tim 4:15). Good intentions do not replace good craft.
45713: What would it mean to get better at this?
45714: Who could mentor or train me?
45715: Am I using 'it's for God' as an excuse for careless work?
45717: Without love even spectacular gifts are 'nothing' (1 Cor 13:1-3). Love asks what actually helps the other person, not what makes me look useful.
45718: Whom does this gift actually serve?
45719: Would I still do it if no one noticed?
45720: Is my motive love, fear, or a wish to be admired?
45722: Spirit gifts build up the church (1 Cor 14:12); daily work serves neighbours and the common good (Gal 6:10, Jer 29:7). Both are real service to God.
45723: How does this build up my church family?
45724: How does it serve people outside the church?
45725: Am I seeking the welfare of my city through it?
45727: Work done with excellence and integrity 'adorns' the gospel (Titus 2:10) and makes people curious (1 Pet 2:12). When questions come, be ready to speak gently about your hope (1 Pet 3:15).
45728: Does the quality and honesty of my work speak well of Christ?
45729: Am I ready to explain my hope when asked?
45730: Am I respecting people's freedom, or pressuring them?
45732: God looked at his work and called it good, then rested (Gen 1:31, Gen 2:2-3). Moses saw the finished tabernacle and blessed the workers (Exod 39:43). End with thanks and Sabbath, not with anxiety about results.
45733: Can I stop and call good work good?
45734: Do I measure my worth by results?
45735: What will I thank God for in this work today?
45736: Does my work or gift have to 'lead to evangelism' to matter to God?
45737: Answer honestly. The results present the main Christian views fairly. Most mature believers end up holding several of them together.

45771: Expression and witness are both real
45772: Your gift honours God in itself, because it reflects the creativity of the God whose image you bear, and it serves others. That same faithful work is also a witness: people see good works and glorify the Father (Matt 5:16). Many evangelical and Reformed teachers (Keller, Crouch, Stott) and Catholic and Orthodox traditions hold this integrated view. Keep both: do the work well and in love, and be ready to speak when asked.
45773: Your work is service to your neighbour
45774: Ordinary work is not second-class. Paul tells workers to serve 'as for the Lord' (Col 3:23-24), and Luther taught that God feeds and cares for the world through people's daily callings. You do not need to attach a sermon to a well-made table or a carefully kept account for it to please God. Release the guilt; offer the work with thanks.
45776: Your life and work have earned you trust; now let your words follow. Paul asks how people will believe without hearing (Rom 10:14-15), and Peter says to be ready to give a reason for your hope, with gentleness and respect (1 Pet 3:15). This is not a betrayal of good work but its natural partner. Evangelicals rightly insist that silence about Christ is not neutral.
45778: Love that is conditional on conversion is not yet the love Jesus showed. He healed ten lepers knowing nine would not return (Luke 17:11-19), and he looked at the rich young man and loved him though he walked away (Mark 10:21). Serve people because they bear God's image. Keep sharing Christ, but as a gift offered to a friend, not as a sale closed with a customer.
45779: Gifts are for building up the body
45780: Spirit gifts are given 'for the common good' (1 Cor 12:7) and to build up the church (1 Cor 14:12, Eph 4:12). Encouraging, teaching, helping and giving within the church are not lesser than evangelism; a loving, united church is itself a witness to the world (John 13:35, John 17:21).
45782: Some careful evangelical teachers (for example DeYoung and Gilbert, Piper) argue that because people face eternal judgement and salvation, the church's distinct mission is to proclaim Christ and make disciples. This is a serious view rooted in texts like Matt 28:18-20 and 2 Cor 5:20. Notice, though, that these same writers also affirm that a Christian's ordinary work and good deeds please God; they distinguish what the church as an institution is sent to do from everything a Christian may rightly do. Consider also the resurrection hope of a renewed creation (Rom 8:19-21).
45783: Rest: your worth is not your output
45784: If your gift has become a way to feel valuable, God's first answer is Sabbath. Even the holy work of the tabernacle stopped for rest (Exod 31:12-17). You are loved before you are useful. Receive that, then return to your gift with freedom rather than pressure.
45785: How Christians have thought about gifts, work and witness
45787: God fills Bezalel with his Spirit for skill in craft and gives Oholiab to help him (Exod 31:1-6). This is the traditional early date for the exodus; many scholars prefer about 1260 BC. Either way, Israel's memory puts artistic skill at the heart of worship.
45789: The Chronicler describes David appointing families of skilled singers and players, led by Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, to 'prophesy' with instruments (1 Chr 25:1-7). Music becomes a permanent, trained ministry.
45791: The *Epistle to Diognetus* (second century, date uncertain) says Christians live in ordinary cities, follow local customs in dress and food, and yet show a remarkable way of life. Early Christians kept their trades, though writers like Tertullian (*On Idolatry*) said they must refuse work that served idol worship.
45793: The *Rule of St Benedict* (about 530) orders monastic life around set hours of prayer and set hours of manual work and reading; chapter 48 says idleness is the enemy of the soul. The famous motto 'ora et labora' (pray and work) summarises this rhythm, but the phrase itself is not in the Rule and seems to date from the nineteenth century.
45795: Abbot Suger dedicates the rebuilt choir of Saint-Denis near Paris, its light and coloured glass meant to lift the mind from material beauty to God. Medieval cathedrals were the work of thousands of skilled craftsmen, yet the 'religious' life of monks and clergy was ranked above lay work. This hierarchy goes back to writers like Eusebius of Caesarea (*Demonstration of the Gospel* 1.8, early fourth century), who described a 'perfect' life given wholly to God and a lower, 'permitted' life for those who farm, trade and marry.
45797: In his 1520 treatises Luther argues that all baptised Christians are priests and that the works of monks and priests are no holier in God's sight than the work of a farmer in the field or a woman in her household. Later he describes daily callings as 'masks of God' through which God cares for the world. The popular line about God 'milking the cows through the milkmaid' paraphrases this idea and is usually traced to Gustaf Wingren's summary, not to a confirmed Luther text.
45799: In the final edition of the *Institutes* (3.10.6), Calvin says God has assigned each person a calling, like a sentry post, so that no one drifts through life, and that no task is so humble that it does not shine before God when done in obedience.
45801: William Perkins's *A Treatise of the Vocations or Callings of Men* (published 1603) distinguishes a 'general calling' to be a Christian from a 'particular calling' to a trade, and teaches that both serve God and the common good. Later Puritans such as Richard Baxter developed this in detail.
45803: Philipp Jakob Spener's *Pia Desideria* calls for heart-religion, Bible study groups and active lay faith. Pietism energised missions, education and care for orphans (Francke at Halle), and also taught many to judge activities by their direct spiritual usefulness.
45805: J. S. Bach becomes cantor in Leipzig. He often headed scores 'J.J.' (Jesu juva, 'Jesus, help') and ended them 'S.D.G.' (Soli Deo gloria, 'to God alone the glory'), on secular pieces as well as church works. In his Bible he noted that 1 Chronicles 25 is the foundation of God-pleasing church music.
45807: John Wesley's sermon on money (preached from the 1740s and printed around 1760) urges Christians to gain all they can by honest work, save all they can and give all they can. Methodism joined fervent evangelism with schools, medicine and help for the poor.
45809: Charles Finney's *Lectures on Revivals of Religion* argue that revival is the right use of appropriate means, defending techniques such as the 'anxious bench'. Revivalism made the conversion of individuals the measure of the church's success, though Finney himself also backed abolition and social reform.
45811: D. L. Moody preaches and Ira Sankey sings across Britain (1873-1875). Sankey's gospel songs were written and sung to prepare hearers for the sermon. Moody famously described the world as a wrecked ship and his task as saving as many as he could in the lifeboat, an image that shaped generations of evangelical priorities.
45812: The World Missionary Conference in Edinburgh, chaired by John R. Mott, gathers Protestant missions with the hope of evangelising the world 'in this generation'. Missions then included schools, hospitals and translation alongside preaching.
45814: After the Fundamentalist-Modernist controversies of the 1920s, many conservative Protestants withdrew from cultural and social engagement, which they linked with the liberal 'social gospel'. Historian Timothy L. Smith called this the 'great reversal', and sociologist David Moberg made the phrase famous in his 1972 book. Premillennial expectation of the end often reinforced the focus on saving souls.
45816: In an address at Eastbourne on 23 April 1942, Dorothy L. Sayers argues that the church has failed workers by caring only that they are honest and come to church, not that their work is good. Work should be the full expression of a person's God-given faculties. Her book *The Mind of the Maker* (1941) links human creativity to the Trinity.
45817: Billy Graham's Los Angeles campaign launches decades of mass evangelism. Music, film, broadcasting and celebrity testimony were enlisted for the crusades, making 'using your gift for the gospel' a powerful and inspiring model for millions.
45819: Larry Norman's song 'Why Should the Devil Have All the Good Music?' (1972) captures the Jesus-music movement that grew into the Contemporary Christian Music industry. Debates followed for decades over whether Christian musicians were ministers who must mention Jesus or artists free to write about all of life.
45821: Francis Schaeffer argues that art is not justified only by being a vehicle for evangelism; a Christian's creativity is valuable as the work of a creature made in God's image. With his friend Hans Rookmaaker he encouraged evangelicals to take the arts seriously.
